newsitem.title: SPAIN: SOCCER-RELEGATION TUSSLE TAKES SPOTLIGHT IN SPAIN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-RELEGATION TUSSLE TAKES SPOTLIGHT IN SPAIN.

text.p: With all the honours decided, attention in the last weekend of the Spanish league will be focused on the fight to avoid relegation to the second divsion.
Ironically each of the three teams threatened with the drop face the three top sides in the league.
Celta Vigo play champions Real Madrid, runners-up Barcelona travel to Rayo Vallecano, and third-placed Deportivo Coruna host Extremadura.
The last of four automatic relegation places is still unfilled, as is the berth for the play-off against second divsion Mallorca.
A further side, Oviedo, are safe from automatic relegation but could find themselves in the play-off if they lose the Asturian derby game to rivals Sporting Gijon.
Sorting out the implications of results could cause fans quite a headache on Sunday evening.
Spain's scoring system means that results of the regular season games between teams is used before goal difference to determine final standings if sides finish level on points.
If three or more teams finish level, the calculations can become complex.
Similar tussles at the other other end of the table inevitably bring talk of bonuses paid to third parties.
Such bonuses are banned in Spain, although nobody doubts that they are routinely used at the end of the season.
The more modest clubs at the bottom of the division are not able to pay out big sums, a situation that has prompted a jovial interchange of offers during the week.
The Extremadura club have promised the Barcelona and Real Madrid players a leg of the renowned ham from their rural base for winning this weekend's games.
"That's nice," said Real defender Fernando Hierro.
The Celta squad responded with an offer of spider crabs from their home city, which is one of Spain's biggest fishing ports.
Madrid-based Rayo Vallecano could only come up with a promise of chocolates.
Of the three sides Extremadura in theory face the toughest job.
Only a win will be enough for the first-division new boys, and they are the only side not playing at home.
But Deportivo have been wracked by injuries and international duty, and have even appealed to have the game postponed because only 12 first team players will be available.
Losing to Extremadura could also mean disaster for Deportivo's local rivals, Celta.
There were widespread accusations of game-throwing in a similar case last month after Real Betis lost to Sporting Gijon, a result that badly affected Betis' rivals Sevilla.
Sevilla lost the following day, and will definitely be relegated alongside Hercules and Logrones.
But whereas four teams go straight down, only two second division teams come up -- champions Merida and second-placed Salamanca.
Third-placed Mallorca take a play-off slot, while Eibar take 150 million pesetas ($1.03 million) compensation for not having a crack at promotion despite finishing fourth.
As a result the Spanish first division will be reduced from 20 to 22 teams.
The enlargement occurred in the summer of 1995, when Celta and Sevilla were both condemned to the third division for accountancy irregularities.
Two relegation-bound teams were therefore reprieved, but protests in Sevilla and Vigo led to the original decision being quashed, and all four teams stayed in the top flight.
Ironically Celta could now join Sevilla as one of the teams obliged to drop out of the limelight.
